scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: Keep your lamps ready
theme: The bridegroom’s delay gives us time to practise the love we cannot borrow at his coming.
introduction: Ten virgins wait for a wedding, carrying lamps that look much alike. All grow drowsy; all hear the midnight cry. The difference lies in the oil they have brought. The Fathers read the oil through good works, mercy, and the gladness of a conscience turned toward God. Their interpretations ask what sustains our outward profession of faith when applause falls silent and the waiting ends.
hero_alt: Ten virgins with oil lamps await the bridegroom at a golden doorway under a midnight-blue sky, in mosaic, stained glass and gold leaf.
closing_title: The oil we can gather today
closing: Chrysostom places the poor before us here and now, where help can still be given. Augustine asks where our joy rests when no one praises us. Jerome presses the connection between the Lord we confess and the works we do. Their readings leave us with work close at hand: answer a need, examine a motive, and let faith take shape in conduct while the door remains open.

Verse 1 preserves the Douay-Rheims phrase "the bridegroom and the bride"; verse 13 retains its shorter ending without adding a phrase from the Catena biblical text. Patristic insights and expansions are original summaries of the public-domain Newman translation of the Catena Aurea, not verbatim quotations. Different Fathers offer complementary readings of the oil; these are attributed individually.

verses.text: Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride.
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: Gregory reads the kingdom here as the Church in this present life. Within it, the wise and foolish wait together.
verses.commentary: Gregory begins with the Church as we know it before the final judgment. Christ elsewhere speaks of angels gathering offences out of his kingdom; here too, the kingdom includes people whose lives will receive different judgments. Gregory connects the ten virgins with the bodily senses and with a Church gathered from both sexes. The outward company is shared, while inward readiness differs. His reading prevents us from assuming that belonging to the waiting company already settles the question of how we have lived within it.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–13

verses.text: Five of them were foolish, and five were wise.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: The same outward discipline can have different motives. Augustine distinguishes the wish to please God from the wish to win applause.
verses.commentary: Augustine understands the five virgins through restraint of the five bodily senses. Both groups practise a kind of continence: they hold back from the pleasures that might draw them away. Yet the purpose of that restraint matters. Some seek to please God and find their joy in a conscience turned toward him. Others depend upon the approval of people who see their outward conduct. Augustine therefore locates wisdom and folly within the intention of the person, even where the visible practice looks much the same.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–13

verses.text: The five foolish ones took their lamps but did not take oil with them.
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: Jerome sees a profession of faith without the works of virtue. A lamp can be carried without the provision it needs to burn.
verses.commentary: Jerome distinguishes those who possess oil from those who merely appear to share the same faith. The first join their confession to good works; the others neglect the works of virtue. His explanation follows the contrast within the parable itself: everyone has a lamp, but the provision accompanying it differs. Outward similarity can conceal a serious lack. Jerome does not dismiss the confession of faith. He asks whether that confession has been accompanied by the conduct that belongs to it, so that what is professed is also lived.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–13

verses.text: But the wise took oil in their vessels along with their lamps.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: Augustine finds the oil in the inward gladness of good works. The wise keep that joy in their hearts and consciences.
verses.commentary: Augustine connects the oil with the gladness of a life pleasing to God. The wise take this gladness in their vessels because they keep it within the heart and conscience. Their joy does not require another person to applaud their restraint or certify their goodness. Augustine recalls Paul's counsel that each person should examine his own work and then have grounds for rejoicing in himself rather than in another. The vessel thus directs attention inward, toward the place where conduct is weighed before God rather than displayed for praise.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–13

verses.text: While the bridegroom delayed, they all grew drowsy and slept.
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: Jerome reads their sleep as death, from which they will be awakened. The delay points to the interval between Christ’s first and second coming.
verses.commentary: Jerome understands the sleep of the virgins in relation to death and the resurrection. They sleep because they are dead, yet the description also looks ahead to their being awakened. Both groups pass through this sleep; it does not by itself distinguish the wise from the foolish. The bridegroom's delay expresses the long interval between the Saviour's first coming and his second. Jerome's reading keeps the story's expectation alive across that interval: death is described as sleep because the sleepers will not remain beyond the reach of the coming summons.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–13

verses.text: At midnight a cry rang out: Look, the bridegroom is coming! Go out to meet him.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: For Augustine, midnight expresses an arrival no one expected. The waiting Church is also the bride who will be joined to Christ.
verses.commentary: Augustine reads midnight as the moment when people neither knew nor expected the bridegroom to arrive. He also considers why the summons now speaks of meeting the bridegroom alone. The virgins themselves belong to the bride: the Church is made up of the people gathered into her, just as children run to a mother who is herself their gathered company. The Church is now betrothed. At the marriage, what is mortal will have passed away, and she will be held in an enduring union with her Lord.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–13

verses.text: Then all those virgins rose and trimmed their lamps.
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: All are raised from the sleep of death. Gregory understands the trimming of the lamps as a reckoning of the works of their lives.
verses.commentary: Gregory sees both the elect and the rejected rising from the sleep of death. The summons reaches everyone; the difference between the two groups emerges in what they have brought to that meeting. To trim their lamps is, in his explanation, to reckon up the works for which they hope to receive eternal blessedness. The scene therefore turns from the long common sleep to a personal accounting. Each must face the truth of the life already lived, rather than rely on the fact that all have heard the same awakening cry.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–13

verses.text: The foolish said to the wise: Give us some of your oil, for our lamps have gone out.
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: Works that looked bright to others can prove empty before the Judge. Gregory hears the request for oil as a desperate appeal for outside testimony.
verses.commentary: Gregory explains the failing lamps through the contrast between outward appearance and inward truth. Some works seemed bright to those who watched them, yet lose that brightness when the Judge comes. Those who find themselves empty within then look outside themselves for someone to speak on their behalf. Their neighbours have seen their conduct; perhaps those witnesses can now establish what their own conscience cannot. Gregory presents the request for oil as this appeal for testimony, made by people whose confidence in their visible reputation has failed at the moment of judgment.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–13

verses.text: The wise answered: There might not be enough for us and for you. Go instead to those who sell it, and buy some for yourselves.
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: Chrysostom does not read the refusal as a failure of mercy. The charity another person practised cannot replace the mercy we ourselves refused to give.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom calls the wise virgins merciful and says their mercy is precisely why they are approved. Their refusal therefore cannot be explained by unwillingness to help. At that judgment they cannot supply what the others failed to acquire through their own lives. He connects the oil with charity and aid to the needy, then brings the warning back to the present. The poor are here, where we can help them now. The time for storing this oil is the life in which those needs stand before us.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–13

verses.text: While they went to buy, the bridegroom came. Those who were ready went in with him to the marriage feast, and the door was shut.
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: Jerome reads the closed door as the finality of judgment. The time for doing new works has given way to an account of the old.
verses.commentary: Jerome pauses at the moment when the foolish leave to make the provision they neglected. In his reading, the season for buying has passed: judgment is arriving, and there is no longer room to begin the repentance and works that should have preceded it. What is required now is an account of the life already lived. The shutting of the door gives that warning its final form. After the day of judgment, he says, there is no further opportunity to acquire righteousness through new good works.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–13

verses.text: At last the other virgins also came, saying: Lord, Lord, open to us.
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: Their address is a confession of faith. Jerome asks what the lips can accomplish when the life has contradicted that confession.
verses.commentary: Jerome notices that the latecomers still address the bridegroom as Lord. He calls this confession worthy and recognises it as a sign of faith. Yet the repeated title does not erase the life that has brought them to the closed door. His question is direct: what does it avail to confess with the mouth the one whom a person denies through works? The problem is not that their words name the wrong Lord. It is the division between those words and the conduct that should have answered to them.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–13

verses.text: But he answered: Amen I say to you, I do not know you.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: Augustine contrasts God’s generous mercy before judgment with its severity afterward. Human praise cannot secure admission to God’s joy.
verses.commentary: Augustine observes that the story never says the foolish virgins succeeded in buying oil. Deprived of the praise on which they depended, they return in distress to ask God for entrance. He describes the severity after judgment in relation to the unspeakable mercy available before it. The answer follows divine wisdom: those who acted under the commandments in order to please people, rather than before God, cannot claim the joy they neglected. Augustine's concern remains the inward direction of their deeds, which the admiration of others could never settle.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–13

verses.text: Keep watch, therefore, because you know neither the day nor the hour.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: We do not know the time of Christ’s coming or of our own death. Augustine joins readiness for both in the life we live now.
verses.commentary: Augustine applies the final command to two times hidden from us. We do not know when the bridegroom will come, and each of us is also ignorant of the time of our own falling asleep in death. Preparation for the latter prepares us for the great summons that will awaken everyone. His reading gives the warning a personal urgency without offering a calculation of dates. The unknown hour calls for readiness before death, so that the voice which raises all sleepers will not find us without the provision we needed to make.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–13
